name: [BMS 1] KUL 6 GENETIKA DASAR (LIA)
text:
Basic genetic 
DNA - Gene - Protein -
Chromosome
DR. dr. Lailia Nur Rachma, M. Biomed
Microbiology department, Medical and Health Faculty
Maulana Malik Ibrahim Malang
Glossary
• DNA chemical subs that makes up genetic code. Made up of four 
simple chemical units A, G, C, and T are used to form three 
letter words (codon) that cells can read.
• A chromosome very long piece of DNA. Humans 23 pairs of 
chromosomes. They are numbered 1-22 with the 23rd pair being 
either XX in girls or XY in boys.
• A gene is a stretch of DNA on a chromosome that has the 
instructions for making a product. Each chromosome has many 
genes with humans having over 22,000 genes in all.
• A protein is a product, result from gene works. It is a molecular 
machine that does a specific job. ex: amylase digest food; 
opsins see colors; globins take oxygen to and carbon dioxide 
away from our cells (blood)
Lets make it more concrete.. 
Hemoglobin(Beta Globin )
• The hemoglobin gene (HBB) is located on chromosome 11.
• Chromosome 11 is a little less than 135 million DNA letters long
over 1500 different genes, one of which is HBB gene-rich 
chromosomes
• The HBB gene located near the middle of this chromosome. 
• 1600 or so DNA letters long The actual instructions for making the 
hemoglobin protein are only 444 letters The other letters are used 
to figure out when, where, and how much of the protein to make.
• Human DNA consists of around 3 billion DNA letters Around 4.5% 
of this is chromosome 11 around 0.000015% of human DNA has 
the instructions for hemoglobin.
• The instructions for hemoglobin are written in the three letter words 
(or codons) I mentioned earlier. To understand how these codons 
work, I need to give a brief description of what a protein is.
• Proteins are strings of amino acids stuck together. The number and 
particular order of the 20 different amino acids determines what a 
protein can do. Proteins can range anywhere from 34,350 amino 
acids in the muscle protein titin to less than 100 amino acids in 
proteins like insulin.
• As I said, the instructions for putting a protein together are found in 
the codons of a gene. Each codon tells the cell which amino acid to 
add to the protein. You can see exactly what amino acid each codon 
makes in a chart like this one:
For example…
• the 444 DNA letters of the HBB gene that tells the cell how to make hemoglobin starts out like this:
• ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGAGGAG ATG GTG CAT CTG ACT CCT GAG GAG Each of these codons tells a cell 
which amino acid to add Met-Val-Leu-Thr-Pro-Glu-Glu ...
• This goes on for another 141 amino acids and you have hemoglobin.
• Hemoglobin is a critical protein in our blood. It carries oxygen to and carbon dioxide away from cells. We 
need for the amino acids to be put together just right or we can end up with a disease. Like sickle cell 
anemia.
• Sickle cell anemia is a disease that affects around 72,000 people in the U.S. People with sickle cell anemia 
have a single difference in the 444 letters of their hemoglobin gene instructions. Their gene starts out with:
• ATG GTG CAT CTG ACT CCT GTG GAG Met-Val-Leu-Thr-Pro-Val-Glu sickle cell anemia
• This one difference is enough to cause sickle cell anemia! In other words, a difference of 1 out of 3 billion 
letters can cause the problems of sickle cell anemia. Similar small changes in other genes can cause 
problems like cystic fibrosis, dwarfism..
• So there you have it. Genes and chromosomes are made up of the 4 letters of DNA. And cells read the letters 
found in stretches of DNA called genes to make proteins that help our bodies and minds run properly.
